rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated relative pronouns signal detailed, encompassing discourse: 58:7 details God's knowledge of every conversation, while the broad statement in 29:52 does not repeat ما.
rows.anchor: أنه إذا كان الموطن دالاً على التفصيل والإحاطة كرر الاسم الموصول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭā Hā 20:6 repeats ما while enumerating what belongs to God in the heavens, earth, between them, and beneath the soil; the more general 16:52 does not.
rows.anchor: فكرر (ما) قائلاً: (يعلم ما في السماوات وما في الأرض)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated relative pronoun in 34:1–2 suits their explicit detail about what is in the heavens and earth and what enters, leaves, descends, and ascends; 2:116 summarizes.
rows.anchor: فالتفصيل في هاتين الآيتين واضح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general statement that all in heaven and earth prostrate in 13:15 leaves من unrepeated; 22:18 repeats it while listing celestial and terrestrial beings in detail.
rows.anchor: فلم يكرر الموصول في حين قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In tasbīḥ verses, repeating ما in ما في the heavens and ما in the earth signals that the following passage will single out people on earth; without repetition, it does not.
rows.anchor: أنه إذا كرر الاسم الموصول فقال: (ما في السماوات وما في الأرض) فإنه يريد أن يخص أهل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥadīd does not follow tasbīḥ with talk of earth's people, whereas the opening of Ḥashr moves to the People of the Book; Ḥashr 24 also uses a single ما without such a follow-up.
rows.anchor: فأنت ترى أنه في آيات الحديد لم يعقب التسبيح بالكلام على أهل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṣaff repeats ما in its tasbīḥ opening because it then addresses believers and discusses people on earth, including those who fight in God's cause.
rows.anchor: ويمضي في الكلام على أهل الأرض فكرر (ما)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jumuʿah repeats ما because its following verses discuss the human recipients of the Messenger's mission and others who have not yet joined them.
rows.anchor: ويمضي في الكلام على أهل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Taghābun repeats ما in the tasbīḥ opening and then turns to people, describing their creation and the distinction between unbelievers and believers.
rows.anchor: هو الذي خلقكم فمنكم كافر ومنكم مؤمن والله بما تعملون بصير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tasbīḥ statement in al-Nūr does not repeat من because it is not followed by a specific discussion of earth's inhabitants.
rows.anchor: فلم يكرر (من) إذ لم يعقب التسبيح بالكلام على أهل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In analogous contexts, an added expression is not an omitted word restored by ellipsis; extra wording is chosen to suit the demands of the context.
rows.anchor: وليس عدم ذكره من باب الحذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The extra kāf in 6:47 intensifies address: those deprived of hearing and sight and sealed in heart need extra alerting, and the threatened torment is more severe, requiring greater warning.
rows.anchor: وهذه الزيادة إنما تكون لغرض توكيد الخطاب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He flags an unresolved contrast: Yūnus 10:50 says أرأيتم, while al-Anʿām 6:40 uses أرأيتكم in a seemingly similar situation; this excerpt asks why but gives no answer.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل: (أرأيتكم) كما قال في الآية السابقة، أو كما قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿrāf places benefit before harm, matching its prior ordering of guidance before misguidance and its following mention of good before evil.
rows.anchor: قالوا: إنه حيث تقدم النفع على الضر فلتقدم ما يتضمن النفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yūnus puts harm before benefit because nearby verses dwell on harm and its removal, and the next verse asks about the torment that criminals hasten.
rows.anchor: فقدم الضر على النفع في الآيتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raʿd puts benefit before harm because the preceding verse puts willing submission before coerced submission.
rows.anchor: قالوا: وذلك لتقدم قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabaʾ places benefit first in keeping with the preceding statement that God expands provision before He restricts it.
rows.anchor: قالوا: وذلك لتقدم قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual order names mercy or forgiveness before punishment, as in the cited formulas of forgiveness before chastisement and of God's mercy before severe retribution.
rows.anchor: فقد قيل إنه حيث ذكر الرحمة والعذاب بدأ بذكر الرحمة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet, narrating from God, reports: My mercy preceded My wrath, supporting the usual precedence of mercy.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا جاء قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حكاية عن الله تعالى:

words: يُعَذِّبُ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَغْفِرُ لِمَن يَشَآءُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 5:40 punishment comes first to warn and deter, fitting its surrounding discussion of killing, armed brigands, and theft; earlier lines also place killing before saving.
rows.anchor: وقد خرج عن هذه القاعدة مواضع اقتضت الحكمة فيها تقديم ذكر العذاب ترهيباً وزجراً

words: يُعَذِّبُ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَغْفِرُ لِمَن يَشَآءُ
rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf explains that punishment precedes forgiveness because theft is mentioned before repentance.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت: لم قدم التعذيب عن المغفرة؟ قلت: لأنه قوبل بذلك تقدم السرقة على التوبة

words: يُعَذِّبُ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَرْحَمُ مَن يَشَاءُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 29:21 punishment precedes mercy because the context warns Abraham's people, including Nimrod and his followers, and recounts worldly punishment visited on them.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأنها في سياق إنذار إبراهيم لقومه ومخاطبة نمورد وأصحابه وأن العذاب وقع بهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word فج originally means a path in a mountain or between two mountains.
rows.anchor: أن الفج في الأصل هو الطريق في الجبل أو بين الجبلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anbiyāʾ puts mountain passes before paths because it has just mentioned mountains; Nūḥ reverses the order because it does not mention mountains.
rows.anchor: فلما تقدم في آية الأنبياء ذكر الرواسي وهي الجبال قدم الفجاج لذلك

words: قُتِلْتُمْ فِي سَبِيلِ الله أَوْ مُتُّمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first verse orders killing before death because it specifies fighting in God's way, where killing is expected and martyrdom is superior; the next omits that setting and starts with ordinary death.
rows.anchor: وهو الجهاد قدم القتل إذ هو المناسب لأن الجهاد مظنة القتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The endings distinguish martyrdom, rewarded with forgiveness and mercy, from death or killing generally, which simply leads to gathering before God.
rows.anchor: فلم يزد في غير الشهيد ومن مات على أن يقول:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After crops, livestock precede people in 32:27; the human-food passage in 80:31–32 lists human nourishment before animal fodder.
rows.anchor: فقدم الأنعام على الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word الأب in the food list means fodder or straw for livestock.
rows.anchor: وهو الأبّ أي: التبن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anʿām addresses poor parents facing actual poverty and promises their provision first; al-Isrāʾ addresses those fearing future poverty and promises children's provision first to reassure them that each child has provision.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن الكلام في الآية الأولى موجه إلى الفقراء دون الأغنياء
